strengths: The paper addresses a clear and well-motivated limitation of time-domain saliency maps for time series, building on prior empirical observations (Schröder et al.) with a principled theoretical extension.

The core theoretical contribution—extending Integrated Gradients to complex-valued domains via Wirtinger calculus while preserving completeness and path independence—is derived carefully, with detailed proofs in the appendix (Lemma 4.2, Definition 4.1, derivation via Stokes' theorem analog).

The framework is genuinely general: it unifies multiple transforms (DFT, STFT, DWT, ICA, STL, Complex Cepstrum) under one formalism, and the paper shows formal connections to existing methods (Virtual Inspection Layers as a special case for DFT, Appendix E; MIX as a special case for Haar-DWT, Remark 4.4), which strengthens the claim of generality.

The mechanistic analysis in Section 4.2 (and the synthetic CNN example in Section 3.2) provides an unusually rigorous sanity check: the authors construct a fully interpretable model and prove analytically that Cross-domain IG in the frequency domain recovers the known mechanism, addressing the common critique that saliency methods lack ground-truth validation.

Evaluation is multi-pronged: axiomatic guarantees, mechanistic analysis, three real-world qualitative case studies (PPG heart-rate, EEG seizure detection, TimesFM forecasting) spanning regression/classification/forecasting, quantitative insertion/deletion faithfulness tests, and benchmark comparisons against TIMEX++/TIMING/FreqRISE/VIL, which together offer reasonably convincing evidence.
The paper commits to releasing an open-source library, aiding reproducibility, and includes thorough implementation details/algorithms in the appendix.

Honest and detailed limitations section (linear path, baseline choice, invertibility assumption, gap between qualitative domain-selection and standardized quantitative benchmarks) that does not undersell weaknesses.
weaknesses: The quantitative benchmark results (Table 2) are mixed: Cross-domain IG (Fourier/Cepstrum) is often worse than TIMING on several datasets (e.g., PAM, Boiler, Wafer for Fourier), and the paper's claim of being "consistently stronger than TIMEX++ and competitive with TIMING" is a somewhat generous reading of a table where superiority is inconsistent across domains/datasets; no single transform dominates, so a practitioner must know in advance which transform to pick, which is not automated or guided by the method itself.

The method fundamentally requires an invertible, differentiable transform and manual selection of baseline and explanation domain by the practitioner; this human-in-the-loop dependency is acknowledged as a limitation but is quite consequential — poor domain choice yields "clean-looking but misleading" explanations, and the paper offers no automated or principled way to select/validate domain appropriateness beyond post-hoc faithfulness scores.

Real-world qualitative case studies (PPG, EEG, forecasting), while illustrative, are largely single-example or small-sample demonstrations (e.g., Figure 2 shows two PPG samples, Figure 3/12 show a few EEG examples) rather than systematic quantitative validation across many subjects/sessions; broader statistical support for the qualitative claims (beyond the insertion/deletion numbers in the Appendix) is limited in the main text.

The insertion/deletion faithfulness evaluations (Section 5.2.1, Appendix G) are reasonable but somewhat ad hoc protocol choices (e.g., top-3% feature deletion, single-IC insertion/deletion) without strong justification for these particular thresholds, and lack statistical significance testing or confidence intervals in the main text (though variance is reported in Table 2).

The complex-valued IG derivation, while mathematically interesting, is presented somewhat densely with derivation sketches in the main text and full proofs relegated to appendix; a reader cannot fully verify soundness without extensive appendix cross-referencing, which affects self-containedness of the main paper.

Novelty relative to prior transformed-coordinate IG work (e.g., MIX, VIL) is somewhat incremental: the primary technical novelty is the complex-domain extension and the unification across more transforms, rather than a fundamentally new interpretability paradigm; the paper positions itself as a generalization/unification rather than introducing fundamentally new explanatory power beyond what individual prior domain-specific methods already offered.

No discussion of computational cost quantitatively (e.g., wall-clock time or complexity comparison) despite acknowledging overhead in Remark 4.6; this could matter for practitioners choosing among methods.
